scenes.title: Choose Compute Placement from Workload Constraints
scenes.visual_overview: On the approved slide, titled Choose Compute Placement from Workload Constraints, the numbered panels depict compare region-scale managed services and resilience along with the architecture decisions and failure considerations.
visual_walkthrough: Compare Region-scale managed services and resilience
Explain Local Zones near users and their parent Region dependence
Explain Outposts in customer facilities and service-link requirements
Compare customer-managed on-premises compute and ownership obligations
scenes.visual_example: A hybrid AWS application follows the diagram's choices and validates both its normal workload and relevant degraded or failure condition.
scenes.visual_synthesis: The depicted architecture is usable only after its dependencies, security, routing and recovery are verified.
scenes.narration: This comparison asks us to choose a location before choosing a platform. Read the four panels from left to right. AWS Regions provide the broadest managed-service portfolio and familiar regional resilience options, which suit workloads that can accept the network distance to a Region. The next panel shows Local Zones, which place supported compute and other resources closer to particular users or metropolitan systems. They remain extensions of a parent Region, and not every service or instance type is available locally. The third panel describes AWS Outposts. AWS-managed supported infrastructure runs inside the customer's facility, but the customer must supply a suitable site and connectivity to the parent Region. The fourth panel describes conventional customer-managed on-premises compute, which offers direct physical control at the cost of greater platform and operations responsibility. At the bottom, the takeaway asks us to list data residency, latency, compliance, operations and regional dependencies. A low-latency requirement alone is not enough; the full dependency path, service availability and failure behavior determine the best placement.

scenes.visual_example: A hybrid AWS application follows the diagram's choices and validates both its normal workload and relevant degraded or failure condition.
scenes.visual_synthesis: The depicted architecture is usable only after its dependencies, security, routing and recovery are verified.
scenes.narration: This slide deepens the Outposts architecture using four stages. Start at the first orange panel. AWS supplies and manages the supported Outposts infrastructure, while the customer provides physical space, power and connectivity. That is a shared-responsibility deployment, not an unmanaged local server rack. In the second panel, supported AWS compute and services run near existing local applications and data, reducing some local round trips. But the third panel is the critical dependency: the Outposts service link connects back to the parent AWS Region for management and service communication. Notice the two-way arrows between the rack and the regional cloud. The fourth panel intentionally breaks that path. Some already-running local workloads may continue for a period depending on their dependencies, while control-plane actions, regional services and management operations can become impaired. For SAP design questions, investigate application dependencies before assuming the workload is disconnected-capable. Validate service-link capacity, site readiness, local communication and what happens during both disconnection and restoration.

scenes.visual_overview: On the approved slide, titled Outposts Racks: Service Link versus Local Gateway, the numbered panels depict follow service link from outposts rack to parent region and control-plane services along with the architecture decisions and failure considerations.
visual_walkthrough: Follow service link from Outposts rack to parent Region and control-plane services
Trace local gateway between rack subnets and the customer on-premises network
Explain local routing, addressing, BGP and supported modes
Distinguish Outposts servers' local network interfaces
scenes.visual_example: A hybrid AWS application follows the diagram's choices and validates both its normal workload and relevant degraded or failure condition.
scenes.visual_synthesis: The depicted architecture is usable only after its dependencies, security, routing and recovery are verified.
scenes.narration: There are two different networking roles on this slide, and confusing them leads to poor hybrid designs. Start in the first panel. The service link joins the Outposts rack to the parent AWS Region and supports control-plane and service communication. In the second panel, follow the path from the Outposts rack through its local gateway to the on-premises network. The local gateway is for supported local network connectivity between rack resources and the customer environment; it is not simply another name for the service link. Now examine the third panel, where routing, addressing and BGP configuration are listed. These have to match the supported Outposts rack routing modes and the customer's network, including appropriate return routes and avoiding conflicting CIDRs. The last panel separately shows Outposts servers. Those use local network interfaces and must not be assumed to follow the same rack local gateway design. The bottom reminder joins the decisions: use service link for regional dependencies, local gateway for rack-to-premises connectivity and the supported server networking model where applicable. Test them as separate paths.

scenes.title: Local Zones: Nearby Resources and Regional Dependencies
scenes.visual_overview: On the approved slide, titled Local Zones: Nearby Resources and Regional Dependencies, the numbered panels depict enable a supported local zone and extend a vpc with its subnet along with the architecture decisions and failure considerations.
visual_walkthrough: Enable a supported Local Zone and extend a VPC with its subnet
Place eligible compute and storage near users to reduce the relevant latency
Check location-specific service and instance availability
Account for parent Region routes, transfers, capacity and disaster recovery
scenes.visual_example: A hybrid AWS application follows the diagram's choices and validates both its normal workload and relevant degraded or failure condition.
scenes.visual_synthesis: The depicted architecture is usable only after its dependencies, security, routing and recovery are verified.
scenes.narration: The center of this architecture shows a Local Zone close to users, with an AWS parent Region underneath. Begin with the first cyan callout on the left. You enable an available Local Zone and create a subnet there as an extension of a VPC; it is not a separate full AWS Region. In the upper-right panel, place supported compute and storage near end users or local systems so that the most latency-sensitive portion of the application can run nearby. That only improves latency when the relevant traffic and state stay on the shorter path. The lower-left panel warns that service availability and instance families vary by location; check supported resources before designing the workload. Finally, the lower-right callout traces dependencies back toward the parent Region. Consider regional services, data movement, cross-zone transfers, failure recovery and their effect on latency and cost. If every request still needs a distant regional database, the expected performance gain may disappear. Select a Local Zone for a measured end-to-end latency requirement, not just because its map pin is nearer.
